The Navagraha: Meet the Nine Planets of Vedic Astrology

Meet the Navagraha — the nine grahas of Vedic astrology, including shadow planets Rahu and Ketu — and how they shape Dashas and planetary hours.

Key Takeaways

  • •The Navagraha are the nine grahas of Vedic astrology: Surya, Chandra, Mangal, Budha, Guru, Shukra, and Shani, plus the lunar nodes Rahu and Ketu.
  • •Rahu and Ketu are not physical bodies but mathematically calculated points where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic — yet Jyotish treats them as full "shadow planets," or Chhaya Grahas.
  • •Each graha carries its own mythology and core theme, and together they rule the seven-day week and the planetary-hours system.
  • •The same nine grahas, weighted by a Nakshatra-based sequence, form the Vimshottari Dasha — the primary timing system used to read a Vedic birth chart.

Open a Vedic birth chart for the first time and one word appears more than any other: graha. Every house, every aspect, every yoga in the chart ultimately comes back to nine of them — the Navagraha, or "nine seizers," the planetary forces classical Jyotish treats as the primary shapers of a life. Some are familiar from any astronomy textbook. Two are not physical bodies at all. Understanding all nine, individually and as a set, is close to a prerequisite for reading a Vedic chart with any confidence.

What Are the Navagraha?

Navagraha comes from Sanskrit: nava (nine) and graha (seizer, or that which grasps). The term reflects an old idea in Jyotish — that these nine points in the sky don't merely sit passively overhead but actively "grasp" or influence the affairs of the world and the individual, for better or worse, depending on their placement and strength in a chart. Seven of the nine correspond to visible bodies our ancestors could track with the naked eye: the Sun, the Moon, and the five planets visible without a telescope. The remaining two, Rahu and Ketu, are something else entirely — a distinction worth sitting with before meeting the full set.

It also helps to notice what the Navagraha are *not*. Classical Jyotish never included Uranus, Neptune, or Pluto, since none of the seven visible grahas plus the two nodes needed supplementing to make the system work — those outer bodies simply weren't observable until telescopes existed, long after the Navagraha framework had already matured. Some modern practitioners reference them in a secondary role today, but the nine-graha core has remained essentially unchanged for well over two thousand years.

Meet the Nine Grahas

Each graha carries its own mythology, its own core theme, and its own role in a chart. Here is the full set, in the order most commonly used to describe them:

  • Surya (Sun) — the soul, willpower, and vitality; the king of the Navagraha, associated with the Vedic solar deity of the same name.
  • Chandra (Moon) — the mind, emotion, and instinct; considered the queen, and the graha Jyotish treats as the primary personal placement (Rashi).
  • Mangal (Mars) — courage, drive, and conflict; a fiery warrior planet linked to the deity Kartikeya and to physical energy and assertiveness.
  • Budha (Mercury) — intellect, communication, and commerce; associated with the prince of the grahas and quick, adaptable thinking.
  • Guru (Jupiter) — wisdom, expansion, and dharma; revered as the guru or teacher of the gods, and traditionally the most benefic of the nine.
  • Shukra (Venus) — love, beauty, and material comfort; teacher of the opposing forces in Vedic myth, and ruler of relationships and pleasure.
  • Shani (Saturn) — discipline, delay, and karma; often misunderstood as purely malefic, but classically understood as a strict but fair teacher who rewards patience and hard work.
  • Rahu (North Node) — obsession, ambition, and worldly desire; a shadow planet with no physical body, tied to illusion (Maya) and unchecked craving.
  • Ketu (South Node) — detachment, spirituality, and past-life karma; Rahu's counterpart, associated with liberation (Moksha) and sudden endings.

Rahu and Ketu: The Two Shadow Planets

Rahu and Ketu are the detail that most surprises newcomers to Jyotish. Astronomically, they are not planets, moons, or any kind of physical body at all — they are the two points where the Moon's orbital path crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit around the Sun, known in Western astronomy as the ascending and descending lunar nodes. Rahu marks the point where the Moon crosses from south to north of the ecliptic; Ketu marks the opposite crossing, always sitting exactly 180 degrees from Rahu. Both are purely mathematical, calculated positions, moving continuously (and, unusually, backward relative to the other grahas) through the zodiac.

Despite having no physical mass, Rahu and Ketu are treated in Jyotish as full grahas with real predictive weight — classified as Chhaya Grahas, or "shadow planets." The reasoning is rooted in classical mythology: the story of the demon Svarbhanu, beheaded by Vishnu after tricking his way into a sip of the gods' nectar of immortality, with the severed head becoming Rahu and the body becoming Ketu. Because both halves had already tasted immortality, neither could truly die — they persist in the sky as points, forever tied to eclipses, since an eclipse occurs precisely when the Sun or Moon crosses paths with one of these two nodes. That mythic origin is also why Rahu and Ketu are so strongly associated with karma, destiny, and unfinished business: a story about desire, deception, and a fate that could not be undone.

Why include non-physical points as "planets" at all?

It can feel inconsistent to place mathematical points alongside the Sun, Moon, and five visible planets. Classical Jyotish resolves this by defining a graha functionally rather than physically: anything that measurably influences the character of time and the individual chart qualifies, whether or not it has mass. Rahu and Ketu meet that bar so consistently in traditional practice that dropping them would leave major chart-timing and karmic themes unaccounted for — which is exactly why they were folded into the Navagraha rather than treated as a separate footnote.

How the Navagraha Shape Timing: Planetary Hours and Dashas

The Navagraha aren't only about personality and mythology — they're the literal scaffolding behind two of the most-used timing systems in Jyotish. The first is day-rulership: each day of the seven-day week is assigned to one of the seven visible grahas (Sunday to the Sun, Monday to the Moon, Tuesday to Mars, and so on), and that same logic extends further into planetary hours, where each daylight and nighttime hour cycles through a fixed sequence of graha rulers. This is the same Vara concept covered in our guide to the Panchang, where the weekday's ruling planet is treated as one of the five limbs that color a given day.

The second, larger-scale system is the Vimshottari Dasha — a fixed 120-year sequence of planetary periods, calculated from the Moon's Nakshatra at birth, that assigns each of the nine grahas a distinct span of years to "rule" a person's life. Jupiter's Dasha runs 16 years, Saturn's 19, Rahu's 18, Ketu's just 7, and so on, all nine adding up to 120 years total. Within each major Dasha, sub-periods (Antardashas) cycle through all nine grahas again in miniature, which is how Jyotish practitioners narrow a broad life theme down to a specific window of months or years. None of this would work without the Navagraha as a defined, ordered set — the Dasha system is, in effect, the nine grahas translated directly into a timeline.

Nine grahas, seven of them visible in the night sky and two of them pure geometry, form the working vocabulary of an entire astrological tradition — the vocabulary used to read a birth chart, name the days of the week, and time the unfolding of a life through Dasha. Learning the Navagraha individually is the first real step toward reading a Vedic chart as more than a diagram; it's the difference between seeing nine dots on a wheel and seeing nine distinct characters, each with a role to play.
